beats.heading: Walker opening
beats.narration_text: Jambo — this is Liam, in for Bear. The ask: two animation clips for a pixel-art mage and a cave wolf — a run that loops and a lunge that commits — keyed as data and checked tick by tick against the game.

props.segment: Keys on the Tick: A Run Cycle and a Wolf Lunge

beats.heading: What got built
beats.narration_text: Two clips: a run and a lunge. The lesson: animation here is timing, not drawing — keys on the physics tick the game reads, with gameplay pinned before the first key.

props.text:
Two clips:
a run, a lunge.
Animation
is drawing.

beats.heading: Before and after, the same tick
beats.narration_text: The same scripted moment twice: the pin's take-lunge scenario at tick forty, before Assignment seven and now. Now a keyed rig stretches mid-lunge with an orange afterimage, in a torch-lit cave. Gameplay is identical on every tick.

shot.visual_intent: Before and after, the same tick

show.event: Before and after, the same tick

beats.heading: The run, in play
beats.narration_text: Now the real game, played by scripted input — real key presses, real engine output. The mage runs, four cells at ten a second, stops, runs, jumps the pit and lands. At quarter speed: on the landing tick, the run starts again at cell zero.

beats.heading: The lunge in both facings, in play
beats.narration_text: The wolf. She stops where it first sees her; it growls, crouching, for thirty-one ticks. She steps back, so the lunge misses — a stretch and a dash, trailing orange ghosts. It recovers. She runs past; it growls again, turns to follow, and lunges right. This one hits. One clip, both facings: code flips the Facing node, the clip keys the rig inside.

shot.visual_intent: The lunge in both facings, in play

show.event: The lunge in both facings, in play

beats.heading: An early cast cancels the growl, in play
beats.narration_text: The one behaviour change. The moment the wolf starts to growl, a click: the fireball leaves on growl tick two and lands on tick twenty-one. No lunge — the wolf goes straight to recovery, and its hitbox never arms.

shot.visual_intent: An early cast cancels the growl, in play

show.event: An early cast cancels the growl, in play

beats.heading: Clip 2: route and source
beats.narration_text: Clip two is a cutout rig, not new art: two regions of the Assignment two wolf, overlapping at the waist, on a hip and a shoulder pivot. The motion reference: Muybridge's galloping dog.

beats.heading: The phase table becomes keys (code)
beats.narration_text: The phase table came from the pin: growl thirty-one ticks, lunge twenty-two, recover thirty-six. The keys follow it, in frames over sixty. Here, the rig's scale: crouch, stretch, overshoot.

beats.heading: The run, cell by cell (result)
beats.narration_text: Tick by tick, in the capture: six, six, six, seven ticks per cell on entry, then five, six, six, seven each loop — the clip wraps on the tick it reaches point four. The read-back: sixteen of sixteen.

beats.heading: One authority (code)
beats.narration_text: One authority. The state machine only calls play: a state's clip starts when the state changes, from zero; flip h stays in code. A structure test scans every script: nothing else writes what a clip keys.

beats.heading: Land, run, cell zero (result)
beats.narration_text: In the capture: falling, then on the landing tick, run — from cell zero, not wherever the last run left off. Eleven structure checks agree.

beats.heading: Pin first
beats.narration_text: Pin first. Before any clip, a test recorded eight scripted scenarios, every physics tick, from real input, at three frame rates. Clips added: unchanged. Wired: unchanged. Then one change, in its own commit.

beats.heading: The change (code)
beats.narration_text: Here it is: a hit that leaves HP during the growl sends the wolf to recover and seeks the clip to the recovery section. Every other phase only loses HP.

props.title: The one behaviour change: a growl hit cancels the lunge

beats.heading: What the pin saw (result)
beats.narration_text: The pin saw it from tick twenty-four: growl to recover, no lunge. The brief expected only that scenario to change; kill changed too, since its first hit lands in a growl. Played, accepted, then re-pinned: two files, sixteen of sixteen at all three rates.

beats.heading: Edges at the phase boundaries
beats.narration_text: Then the edges: real clicks timed to land on a boundary. First or last growl tick: cancel. First or last lunge tick: no cancel. A killing hit wins everywhere. Thirteen of thirteen, at three rates.

beats.heading: Two alignment bugs
beats.narration_text: That found two bugs no read-back could see: a cancel drew clip frame fifty-four, so it now seeks fifty-two; and a growl after a one-tick patrol started at frame one, so both players now run first. This film's capture shows both fixes holding.

beats.heading: Broken on purpose
beats.narration_text: Broken on purpose. Godot three's loop equals true: not caught — four point seven point two loads it as a looping clip anyway. A continuous frame track, a cell past the sheet, a missing node, no cancel: all caught.

beats.heading: The growl window and a second clock
beats.narration_text: Two findings, kept. From sight distance, only a cast in the first twelve growl ticks — a fifth of a second — can cancel. And a second clock: the dead wolf's removal runs on frame time — tick seventy-nine at sixty frames a second, eighty at thirty and one forty-four.

beats.heading: The run: r0 and three dead ends
beats.narration_text: The run took longest. Version zero swapped two frames: a one-pixel hat hop while the planted foot slid thirteen to fifteen pixels and snapped back. Three fixes for the other foot failed.

shot.visual_intent: The run: r0 and three dead ends

show.event: The run: r0 and three dead ends

beats.heading: The run: r1 rejected in play, r2 kept
beats.narration_text: Version one bobbed the body; every hat row landed exactly as predicted, and the author rejected it in play anyway. A correct prediction isn't a good result. Version two, a real four-frame cycle, was kept.

shot.visual_intent: The run: r1 rejected in play, r2 kept

beats.heading: Embers, afterimage, readability
beats.narration_text: Plus a hundred and forty-four embers, and a ghost every three lunge ticks. Version zero was not noticeable; version one is clearly visible, with the mage's contrast measured back up to three point oh seven. The pin stayed eight of eight.

beats.heading: Limitations
beats.narration_text: The limits: the planted foot still slides; the growl window is a fifth of a second, by choice. And this is scripted input — how it feels is the author's call.

beats.heading: Who did what
beats.narration_text: Who did what. The author chose both clips, the interrupt rule and the window, made the run images, and judged everything in play. Claude Code built the pin, clips, tests and upgrades; Claude in chat drafted the documents. Revision f eight six oh f e d.

beats.heading: Verdict
beats.narration_text: The verdict. Built: two clips and a flicker, each owned by one animation player on the physics tick. Measured: a pin the clips never moved, one designed change re-pinned after play, four mutations caught. Open: the sliding foot.

artifactLines: Built: the run clip (4 cells, 10 fps, LOOP_LINEAR, discrete), the lunge rig and clip (89 ticks, LOOP_NONE) and the torch flicker, each owned by one AnimationPlayer on the physics callback; the growl cancel; embers and the afterimage; the pin, edges, read-back, structure and afterimage tests.

Measured: pin 16 / 0 at 30, 60, 144 with the clips wired; the change differs only in hit_growl and kill, re-pinned after play (ff71bbb); edges 13 / 0 at 30, 60, 144; mutations a7-2 to a7-5 caught, a7-1 harmless on 4.7.2.
Judged by the author in play: run r2 kept (r1 rejected), the lunge in both facings, the growl cancel and its 0.2 s window, visual upgrades r1 kept (r0 not noticeable).
Open: in-between frames so the planted foot stops sliding; whether the growl window should be wider.

beats.heading: Your Turn
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's a prompt: Please use Walker to add in-between frames to my mage's run so the planted foot stops sliding. First predict, in pixels, how far the body moves while one cell is held at a hundred and ten pixels a second and ten frames a second; then measure the foot in a windowed Movie Maker strip, and show the behaviour pin still matches tick for tick. The prediction is the point: if your number's wrong, the strip says so first. Liam, in for Bear.
